El diagrama de Voronoi es de las estruct: The Voronoi diagram is one of the most reused structures there is. In epidemiology John Snow used it in 1854, drawing which houses in London had the Broad Street water pump nearer than any other, and with that map he proved that cholera travelled by water. In logistics it defines delivery zones; in telephony, which mast serves you; in biology, the territory of each tree or each nest; in geology, the crystallisation of a metal as it cools. And in graphics it is the generator of anything that looks cellular: scales, skins, cobbles, broken ice.
El dual de este dibujo —unir con una ari: The dual of this drawing — joining with an edge the points whose cells touch — is the Delaunay triangulation, which is a [[av-grafos|graph]] with very good properties: it is the triangulation that avoids sharp triangles. The two constructions are the same information seen from the front and from the back.

Georgi Voronói formalizó el reparto en 1: Georgy Voronoy formalised the division in 1908, though Descartes had already drawn something similar in 1644 when imagining how the stars shared out space. It entered graphics in 1996 thanks to Steven Worley, who published a cellular noise function designed for exactly what you are doing here; that is why this pattern is sometimes called “Worley noise”. And that cholera map of John Snow's is still, a century and a half later, the textbook example of how a well-thought-out drawing wins an argument.
